newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Pugnacious Kulikov -- a believer in force.
newsitem.headline: Pugnacious Kulikov -- a believer in force.

text.p: Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, at the centre of an increasingly vicious Kremlin slanging match, is a pugnacious figure strongly identified with Russia's failed attempt to subdue rebel Chechnya by force.
His accusations against Security Chief Alexander Lebed on Wednesday that his rival was plotting a coup with the aid of Chechen fighters turned a long-running feud into an open war of words.

Kulikov, a stocky 50-year-old four-star general who invariably appears in public in army uniform with rows of medal ribbons on his chest, commands Russia's interior ministry troops, including special units, and the police.
But neither the well-equipped interior ministry troops, responsible for crushing internal unrest in Soviet days, nor the police have performed particularly well in post-Soviet Russia.

Crime has increased steadily, especially through the rise of shady mafia-like criminal gangs, and the interior ministry soldiers were frequently humiliated by determined but lightly armed separatists in Russia's 21-month war in Chechnya.
Kulikov's long involvement in Chechnya put him on collision course with Lebed, who negotiated a peaceful end to the fighting within two months of his appointment this summer.

Lebed said in August that Kulikov should quit, blaming him for military reverses against the rebels, who effectively regained control of the capital Grozny on the eve President Boris Yeltsin's inauguration. The minister offered to resign, but Yeltsin told him to stay.
"I am convinced that a settlement in the republic must be achieved by military means," Kulikov said this summer.

Yeltsin appointed Kulikov Interior Minister in July 1995 in succession to Viktor Yerin. Unlike Yerin, a career policeman, Kulikov came from the military side of the ministry and had held a number of commands in the interior ministry troops since the mid-1970s.
At the time of his appointment he commanded the joint defence and interior ministry troops in Chechnya, which declared itself independent in 1991.
Kulikov, a deputy interior minister since late 1992, remained loyal to Yeltsin during a failed uprising by hardline parliamentarians in Moscow in October 1993.

Kulikov is from the Stavropol region, a fertile farming area in southern Russia where people have little love for neighbouring Chechens. It was also the region where Chechen rebels seized hostages in 1995, prompting Yerin's dismissal.
He is a graduate of the Vladikavkaz Higher All Arms Command School and the prestigious Frunze Military Academy as well as the General Staff Academy.
